# Truth Is One Species of Good

Truth is ONE SPECIES OF GOOD, and not, as is usually supposed, a category distinct from good, and co-ordinate with it.[^1] THE TRUE IS THE NAME OF WHATEVER PROVES ITSELF TO BE GOOD IN THE WAY OF BELIEF, AND GOOD, TOO, FOR DEFINITE, ASSIGNABLE REASONS.[^2] Surely you must admit this, that if there were NO good for life in true ideas, or if the knowledge of them were positively disadvantageous and false ideas the only useful ones, then the current notion that truth is divine and precious, and its pursuit a duty, could never have grown up or become a dogma.[^3] In a world like that, our duty would be to SHUN truth, rather.[^4] But in this world,[^5] certain ideas are not only agreeable to think about, or agreeable as supporting other ideas that we are fond of, but they are also helpful in life's practical struggles.[^6]

[^1]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "truth is ONE SPECIES OF GOOD, and not, as is usually supposed, a category distinct from good, and co-ordinate with it."
[^2]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "THE TRUE IS THE NAME OF WHATEVER PROVES ITSELF TO BE GOOD IN THE WAY OF BELIEF, AND GOOD, TOO, FOR DEFINITE, ASSIGNABLE REASONS."
[^3]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "Surely you must admit this, that if there were NO good for life in true ideas, or if the knowledge of them were positively disadvantageous and false ideas the only useful ones, then the current notion that truth is divine and precious, and its pursuit a duty, could never have grown up or become a dogma."
[^4]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "In a world like that, our duty would be to SHUN truth, rather."
[^5]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "But in this world"
[^6]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "certain ideas are not only agreeable to think about, or agreeable as supporting other ideas that we are fond of, but they are also helpful in life's practical struggles."
=== FILE: What Is Better for Us to Believe Comes Near to a Definition of Truth.md ===

# What Is Better for Us to Believe Comes Near to a Definition of Truth

If there be any life that it is really better we should lead, and if there be any idea which, if believed in, would help us to lead that life, then it would be really BETTER FOR US to believe in that idea, UNLESS, INDEED, BELIEF IN IT INCIDENTALLY CLASHED WITH OTHER GREATER VITAL BENEFITS.[^1]

'What would be better for us to believe'![^2] This sounds very like a definition of truth.[^3] It comes very near to saying 'what we OUGHT to believe': and in THAT definition none of you would find any oddity.[^4] Ought we ever not to believe what it is BETTER FOR US to believe?[^5] And can we then keep the notion of what is better for us, and what is true for us, permanently apart?[^6]

Pragmatism says no, and I, William James,[^7] fully agree with her.[^8] Probably you also agree, so far as the abstract statement goes, but with a suspicion that if we practically did believe everything that made for good in our own personal lives, we should be found indulging all kinds of fancies about this world's affairs, and all kinds of sentimental superstitions about a world hereafter.[^9] Your suspicion here is undoubtedly well founded, and it is evident that something happens when you pass from the abstract to the concrete, that complicates the situation.[^10]

[^1]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "If there be any life that it is really better we should lead, and if there be any idea which, if believed in, would help us to lead that life, then it would be really BETTER FOR US to believe in that idea, UNLESS, INDEED, BELIEF IN IT INCIDENTALLY CLASHED WITH OTHER GREATER VITAL BENEFITS."
[^2]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "'What would be better for us to believe'!"
[^3]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "This sounds very like a definition of truth."
[^4]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "It comes very near to saying 'what we OUGHT to believe': and in THAT definition none of you would find any oddity."
[^5]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "Ought we ever not to believe what it is BETTER FOR US to believe?"
[^6]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "And can we then keep the notion of what is better for us, and what is true for us, permanently apart?"
[^7]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means]] "William James"
[^8]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "Pragmatism says no, and I fully agree with her."
[^9]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "Probably you also agree, so far as the abstract statement goes, but with a suspicion that if we practically did believe everything that made for good in our own personal lives, we should be found indulging all kinds of fancies about this world's affairs, and all kinds of sentimental superstitions about a world hereafter."
[^10]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "Your suspicion here is undoubtedly well founded, and it is evident that something happens when you pass from the abstract to the concrete, that complicates the situation."
=== FILE: The Greatest Enemy of Any One of Our Truths May Be the Rest of Our Truths.md ===

# The Greatest Enemy of Any One of Our Truths May Be the Rest of Our Truths

What is better for us to believe is true UNLESS THE BELIEF INCIDENTALLY CLASHES WITH SOME OTHER VITAL BENEFIT.[^1] Now in real life what vital benefits is any particular belief of ours most liable to clash with?[^2] What indeed except the vital benefits yielded by OTHER BELIEFS when these prove incompatible with the first ones?[^3] In other words, the greatest enemy of any one of our truths may be the rest of our truths.[^4] Truths have once for all this desperate instinct of self-preservation and of desire to extinguish whatever contradicts them.[^5]

[^1]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "what is better for us to believe is true UNLESS THE BELIEF INCIDENTALLY CLASHES WITH SOME OTHER VITAL BENEFIT."
[^2]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "Now in real life what vital benefits is any particular belief of ours most liable to clash with?"
[^3]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "What indeed except the vital benefits yielded by OTHER BELIEFS when these prove incompatible with the first ones?"
[^4]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "In other words, the greatest enemy of any one of our truths may be the rest of our truths."
[^5]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "Truths have once for all this desperate instinct of self-preservation and of desire to extinguish whatever contradicts them."
=== FILE: My Belief in the Absolute Must Run the Gauntlet of All My Other Beliefs.md ===

# My Belief in the Absolute Must Run the Gauntlet of All My Other Beliefs

My belief in the Absolute[^1] (the Absolute of transcendental idealism),[^2] based on the good it does me, must run the gauntlet of all my other beliefs.[^3] Grant that it may be true in giving me a moral holiday,[^4] to let the world wag in its own way.[^5] Nevertheless, as I conceive it,--and let me speak now confidentially, as it were, and merely in my own private person,--it clashes with other truths of mine whose benefits I hate to give up on its account.[^6] It happens to be associated with a kind of logic of which I am the enemy, I find that it entangles me in metaphysical paradoxes that are inacceptable, etc., etc..[^7] But as I have enough trouble in life already without adding the trouble of carrying these intellectual inconsistencies, I personally just give up the Absolute.[^8] I just TAKE my moral holidays; or else as a professional philosopher, I try to justify them by some other principle.[^9]

[^1]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "My belief in the Absolute"
[^2]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#Pragmatism as Mediator Between Empiricism and Religion]] "the Absolute of transcendental idealism"
[^3]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "based on the good it does me, must run the gauntlet of all my other beliefs."
[^4]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "Grant that it may be true in giving me a moral holiday"
[^5]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#Pragmatism as Mediator Between Empiricism and Religion]] "to let the world wag in its own way"
[^6]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "Nevertheless, as I conceive it,--and let me speak now confidentially, as it were, and merely in my own private person,--it clashes with other truths of mine whose benefits I hate to give up on its account."
[^7]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "It happens to be associated with a kind of logic of which I am the enemy, I find that it entangles me in metaphysical paradoxes that are inacceptable, etc., etc.."
[^8]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "But as I have enough trouble in life already without adding the trouble of carrying these intellectual inconsistencies, I personally just give up the Absolute."
[^9]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "I just TAKE my moral holidays; or else as a professional philosopher, I try to justify them by some other principle."

# Our Hypotheses Carry Supernumerary Features That Clash

If I could restrict my notion of the Absolute to its bare holiday-giving value, it wouldn't clash with my other truths.[^1] But we cannot easily thus restrict our hypotheses.[^2] They carry supernumerary features, and these it is that clash so.[^3] My disbelief in the Absolute means then disbelief in those other supernumerary features, for I fully believe in the legitimacy of taking moral holidays.[^4]

[^1]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "If I could restrict my notion of the Absolute to its bare holiday-giving value, it wouldn't clash with my other truths."
[^2]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "But we cannot easily thus restrict our hypotheses."
[^3]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "They carry supernumerary features, and these it is that clash so."
[^4]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "My disbelief in the Absolute means then disbelief in those other supernumerary features, for I fully believe in the legitimacy of taking moral holidays."
=== FILE: Pragmatism Widens the Field of Search for God.md ===

# Pragmatism Widens the Field of Search for God

Pragmatism[^1] has in fact no prejudices whatever, no obstructive dogmas, no rigid canons of what shall count as proof.[^2] She is completely genial.[^3] She will entertain any hypothesis, she will consider any evidence.[^4] It follows that in the religious field she is at a great advantage both over positivistic empiricism, with its anti-theological bias, and over religious rationalism, with its exclusive interest in the remote, the noble, the simple, and the abstract in the way of conception.[^5]

In short, she widens the field of search for God.[^6] Rationalism sticks to logic and the empyrean.[^7] Empiricism sticks to the external senses.[^8] Pragmatism is willing to take anything, to follow either logic or the senses, and to count the humblest and most personal experiences.[^9] She will count mystical experiences if they have practical consequences.[^10] She will take a God who lives in the very dirt of private fact-if that should seem a likely place to find him.[^11]

[^1]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "Pragmatism"
[^2]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "has in fact no prejudices whatever, no obstructive dogmas, no rigid canons of what shall count as proof."
[^3]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "She is completely genial."
[^4]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "She will entertain any hypothesis, she will consider any evidence."
[^5]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "It follows that in the religious field she is at a great advantage both over positivistic empiricism, with its anti-theological bias, and over religious rationalism, with its exclusive interest in the remote, the noble, the simple, and the abstract in the way of conception."
[^6]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "In short, she widens the field of search for God."
[^7]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "Rationalism sticks to logic and the empyrean."
[^8]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "Empiricism sticks to the external senses."
[^9]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "Pragmatism is willing to take anything, to follow either logic or the senses, and to count the humblest and most personal experiences."
[^10]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "She will count mystical experiences if they have practical consequences."
[^11]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "She will take a God who lives in the very dirt of private fact-if that should seem a likely place to find him."
=== FILE: Pragmatism's Only Test of Probable Truth Is What Works Best.md ===

# Pragmatism's Only Test of Probable Truth Is What Works Best

Pragmatism[^1]'s only test of probable truth is what works best in the way of leading us, what fits every part of life best and combines with the collectivity of experience's demands, nothing being omitted.[^2] If theological ideas should do this, if the notion of God, in particular, should prove to do it, how could pragmatism possibly deny God's existence?[^3] She could see no meaning in treating as 'not true' a notion that was pragmatically so successful.[^4] What other kind of truth could there be, for her, than all this agreement with concrete reality?[^5]

But you see already how democratic she is.[^6] Her manners are as various and flexible, her resources as rich and endless, and her conclusions as friendly as those of mother nature.[^7]

[^1]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "Pragmatism"
[^2]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "Her only test of probable truth is what works best in the way of leading us, what fits every part of life best and combines with the collectivity of experience's demands, nothing being omitted."
[^3]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "If theological ideas should do this, if the notion of God, in particular, should prove to do it, how could pragmatism possibly deny God's existence?"
[^4]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "She could see no meaning in treating as 'not true' a notion that was pragmatically so successful."
[^5]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "What other kind of truth could there be, for her, than all this agreement with concrete reality?"
[^6]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "But you see already how democratic she is."
[^7]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#The True Is the Good in the Way of Belief]] "Her manners are as various and flexible, her resources as rich and endless, and her conclusions as friendly as those of mother nature."
